section.title: The Sabbath Year and the Firstborn
section.sectionRationale: This chapter continues the statutes shaping Israel's distinctive social economy, legislating a periodic release of debts and servants and consecrating every firstborn animal to the LORD, so that generosity and God's ownership of all things were built into Israel's very calendar.
section.thesis: Moses legislates a seventh-year release of debts and Hebrew servants, commanding open-handed generosity toward the poor precisely because Israel would always have need among them, and consecrates every firstborn male of the flock and herd to the LORD as a reminder of His own claim on the firstborn.
section.frameNote: Four movements: canceling debts every seven years; opening your hand to the poor; freeing Hebrew servants generously; and the firstborn of the flock and herd set apart to the LORD.

verses.text: At the end of every seven years you must cancel debts.

This is the manner of {{shemittah|remission}}: Every creditor shall cancel what he has loaned to his neighbor. He is not to collect anything from his neighbor or brother, because the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed.
You may collect something from a foreigner, but you must forgive whatever your brother owes you.
There will be no poor among you, however, because the LORD will surely bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess as an inheritance,
if only you obey the LORD your God and are careful to follow all these commandments I am giving you today.
When the LORD your God blesses you as He has promised, you will lend to many nations but borrow from none; you will rule over many nations but be ruled by none.

units.label: Open your hand to the poor
units.note: he will cry out to the LORD

verses.text: If there is a poor man among your brothers within any of the gates in the land that the LORD your God is giving you, then you are not to harden your heart or shut your hand from your poor brother.
Instead, you are to {{patach|open}} your hand to him and freely loan him whatever he needs.

Be careful not to harbor this wicked thought in your heart: “The seventh year, the year of release, is near,” so that you look upon your poor brother begrudgingly and give him nothing. He will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.
Give generously to him, and do not let your heart be grieved when you do so. And because of this the LORD your God will bless you in all your work and in everything to which you put your hand.
For there will never cease to be poor in the land; that is why I am commanding you to open wide your hand to your brother and to the poor and needy in your land.
If a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, is sold to you and serves you six years, then in the seventh year you must set him {{chophshi|free}}.
And when you release him, do not send him away empty-handed.
You are to furnish him liberally from your flock, your threshing floor, and your winepress. You shall give to him as the LORD your God has blessed you.
Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you; that is why I am giving you this command today.
But if your servant says to you, ‘I do not want to leave you,’ because he loves you and your household and is well off with you,
then take an awl and pierce it through his ear into the door, and he will become your servant for life. And treat your maidservant the same way.
Do not regard it as a hardship to set your servant free, because his six years of service were worth twice the wages of a hired hand. And the LORD your God will bless you in all you do.

units.label: The firstborn set apart to the LORD

verses.text: You must set apart to the LORD your God every firstborn male produced by your herds and flocks. You are not to put the firstborn of your oxen to work, nor are you to shear the firstborn of your flock.
Each year you and your household are to eat it before the LORD your God in the place the LORD will choose.
But if an animal has a defect, is lame or blind, or has any serious flaw, you must not sacrifice it to the LORD your God.
Eat it within your gates; both the ceremonially unclean and clean may eat it as they would a gazelle or a deer.
But you must not eat the blood; pour it on the ground like water.

shemittah.gloss: Release, remission, a dropping or letting fall. Names the seventh-year cancellation of debts, a structural, built-in reset preventing poverty from becoming permanent and inescapable within the community.

patach.gloss: To open. Used of the hand opened wide toward the poor, an image of deliberate, generous, unclenched giving rather than the closed fist of a hardened heart.

chophshi.gloss: Free, released from servitude. Describes the mandatory release of a Hebrew servant after six years, grounded explicitly in Israel's own memory of being freed from slavery in Egypt.

basic.context: Moses establishes a seventh-year release of debts and Hebrew servants, commands open-handed generosity toward the poor because need would never fully disappear, and consecrates every firstborn male animal to the LORD as an ongoing reminder of His prior claim on all Israel possesses.
basic.hermeneutics: This is specific social and economic legislation for Israel's agrarian covenant community, a real structural safeguard against permanent poverty and servitude. Its underlying principles, generosity, periodic release from crushing debt, and recognizing God's prior claim on all we have, remain abiding truths even though its precise mechanisms belonged to Israel's particular society.
basic.originalLanguages: The shemittah, release, cancels debts structurally every seventh year, preventing poverty from calcifying into permanence. Israel is commanded to patach, open, their hand freely to the poor, and to set every servant chophshi, free, after six years, grounded explicitly in their own history as slaves redeemed from Egypt.
basic.typology: The sabbatical release of debts and servants foreshadows the ultimate release from the debt of sin accomplished in Christ, and the year of the LORD's release that Jesus announces as fulfilled in Himself, quoting Isaiah's jubilee language, Luke 4:18-19.
basic.christ: Jesus opens His ministry by announcing 'the year of the LORD's favor,' Luke 4:18-19, language rooted in the sabbatical and jubilee release traditions of texts like this one, proclaiming Himself the true fulfillment of release from every debt, especially the debt of sin.
basic.god: God structures an entire economic system around generosity and periodic release, refusing to let poverty or servitude become permanent, and He grounds Israel's own generosity in their memory of being redeemed from slavery, showing that grace received is meant to overflow into grace given.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 4:18-19 records Jesus announcing the year of the LORD's favor, echoing this passage's sabbatical release language. Mark 14:7 echoes verse 11's realism that the poor will always be present. 2 Corinthians 8:9 grounds Christian generosity in Christ's own self-giving. Matthew 18:23-35 parables the forgiveness of an enormous debt.
basic.oneStory: This chapter builds structural, recurring generosity into Israel's calendar, refusing to let poverty or servitude become permanent, and rooting all of it in the memory of their own redemption from slavery. That pattern of grace received overflowing into grace given anticipates and is fulfilled in Christ's own proclamation of ultimate release from the far greater debt of sin.

context.literary:
The chapter is shaped by the number seven and by two recurring words, "release" and "bless." The release of debts at the end of seven years, verses 1 to 6, is followed by a warning not to let that release make lenders stingy, verses 7 to 11, and then by the release of servants in the seventh year, verses 12 to 18. The last section, verses 19 to 23, turns to the firstborn animals, which also belong to a yearly rhythm of eating "before the LORD." Blessing is promised again and again, verses 4, 6, 10, 14 and 18, so that every act of release is framed by the assurance that God will not let the generous be the poorer for it.

The heart of the chapter is verses 7 to 11, a small sermon within the law. It moves from the heart to the hand and back again: do not harden your heart or shut your hand, verse 7; open your hand, verse 8; guard your heart against a wicked thought, verse 9; do not let your heart be grieved, verse 10; open wide your hand, verse 11. Deuteronomy does not only regulate the transaction; it addresses the inner attitude that makes the transaction generous or grudging.

The chapter holds a deliberate tension. Verse 4 says, "There will be no poor among you," and verse 11 says, "there will never cease to be poor in the land." The one states what obedience under God's blessing could produce; the other states what Israel will actually face, and both drive the same command to open the hand.

In the flow of Deuteronomy, chapters 14:22 to 16:17 form a block of laws organised around sacred time, and many interpreters read that block as an unfolding of the Sabbath command. Chapter 15 is its centre, applying the rhythm of the seventh day to the seventh year. The motive of verse 15, "Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt," is the very motive Deuteronomy gives for the weekly Sabbath, Deuteronomy 5:15.
context.historical:
Debt in ancient Israel was usually the debt of a farming family after a failed harvest, a sickness or a death. A loan of seed or grain was secured by a pledge, and if the debt could not be repaid, land could be lost and family members could be sold into service to work off what was owed. The pattern is visible later in Nehemiah 5, where families mortgaged fields and saw their children enslaved to pay debts and taxes.

Other ancient Near Eastern societies knew debt release. Old Babylonian kings sometimes issued edicts of "justice" cancelling certain debts and freeing debt slaves, usually at the start of a reign, and the Laws of Hammurabi limited a family member's debt service to three years. The Hebrew word for "liberty" in the Jubilee law of Leviticus 25:10 is related to the Akkadian term for such releases. What is different in Israel is that the release is fixed in the calendar by God, not granted at a king's pleasure. It comes every seventh year whether or not any ruler wishes it, because "the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed," verse 2.

The distinction between "your brother" and "a foreigner" in verse 3 reflects this setting. The foreigner, nokri, is not the resident alien protected elsewhere, but an outsider, often a trader, whose loans were commercial rather than a lifeline for a struggling neighbour. The release was aimed at poverty within the covenant family.

The law's warning in verse 9 proved realistic. Later Jewish teachers record that lenders refused credit as the seventh year approached, and the sage Hillel introduced a legal device, the prozbul, that transferred debts to the court so they could still be collected. The very temptation Moses named became the occasion for a workaround. The servant law also shows development. Exodus 21:7 says a daughter sold as a servant did not go free like the men, but Deuteronomy 15:12 and 17 extend the release and the provisions to "a man or a woman."
context.canonical:
The chapter builds on earlier law and is reused throughout Scripture. Exodus 21:2-6 first set the six years of service and the pierced ear, and Exodus 23:10-11 made the seventh year a fallow year so that "the poor among your people may eat." Leviticus 25 adds the Jubilee and insists that an Israelite who sells himself must be treated "as a hired worker," because "the Israelites are My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt," Leviticus 25:40-42. Deuteronomy 31:10-11 ties the seventh year to a public reading of the law at the Feast of Tabernacles, "in the year of remission of debt."

Israel's failure to keep the release became part of the case for exile. In Jeremiah 34, Zedekiah's Jerusalem proclaims freedom for Hebrew slaves and then takes them back. The LORD quotes this law, "Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother," Jeremiah 34:14, and answers with grim irony, "I proclaim freedom for you ... freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine," Jeremiah 34:17. The Chronicler says the land "enjoyed its Sabbath rest" during the exile, 2 Chronicles 36:21. After the return, Nehemiah confronts creditors, Nehemiah 5:10-11, and the people pledge to "cancel every debt" every seventh year, Nehemiah 10:31.

The prophets turn release into a picture of salvation. Isaiah 58:6 calls for the fast that sets "the oppressed free," and Isaiah 61:1-2 announces "liberty to the captives" and "the year of the LORD's favor." Jesus reads that passage in Nazareth and says it is fulfilled, Luke 4:18-21. He teaches His disciples to pray "forgive us our debts," Matthew 6:12, and tells of a master who "forgave his debt, and released him," Matthew 18:27. He quotes verse 11, "The poor you will always have with you," Mark 14:7, and the first church lives out verse 4, for "there were no needy ones among them," Acts 4:34. The firstborn law stands behind Jesus' presentation in the temple, Luke 2:22-23.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to see that economic life belongs to the covenant. Lending, borrowing, hiring and farming were not outside God's rule; they were among the places where Israel would show whether they had understood their own redemption. The chapter's recurring motive, "Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you," verse 15, means that a creditor who refused release or a master who sent a servant away empty would be acting like Pharaoh.

He also wants to address the heart. The law could have regulated debt release without comment, but Moses anticipates the calculation of verse 9: the year of release is near, so lending now means losing. He names that thought as wicked and warns that the poor man "will cry out to the LORD against you." The intent is not merely compliance but a generous spirit, "do not let your heart be grieved," verse 10.

Moses wants Israel to trust God's blessing. Every command that seems to cost the giver is followed by a promise that the LORD will bless them, verses 10, 14 and 18. Obedience is an act of faith that God, not the tight fist, is the source of provision.

Finally, the firstborn law teaches Israel that the first and best of the herd belongs to God, not to the farmer's labour. They are not to work or shear it, verse 19, but to eat it before Him with their household, turning ownership into worship.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
These are real laws, not narrative, given to regulate an agrarian society living on land God had apportioned to its families. Their precise mechanisms, a fixed seventh year, the release of Hebrew servants, the sacrifice of firstborn animals at the central sanctuary, assumed that society and its temple. No New Testament text commands the church to cancel debts on a seven year cycle, and the sacrifices have been fulfilled in Christ, Hebrews 9:14.

The principles, though, are pressed on believers even more strongly. John asks how the love of God can abide in someone who sees a brother in need but "withholds his compassion," 1 John 3:17, and James rebukes those who wish the poor well without meeting their needs, James 2:15-16. Paul teaches cheerful and generous giving grounded in the grace of Christ, 2 Corinthians 8:9 and 9:7. The idea that God's people should build generosity into the structures of life, not only into occasional feelings, has shaped Christian thinking about lending, wages and debt. Verse 11 also warns against using the permanence of poverty as an excuse; Jesus' words in Mark 14:7 assume the same obligation, "you can help them whenever you want."

debates.question: How does verse 4's promise, 'there will be no poor among you,' relate to verse 11's statement that 'there will never cease to be poor in the land'?

views.label: A conditional ideal followed by a realistic acknowledgment
views.case: Verse 4 is qualified at once by verse 5, 'if only you obey the LORD your God.' It describes what would be true under full obedience and full covenant blessing, while verse 11 acknowledges that, given ongoing human sin and circumstance, poverty would in practice persist, grounding an ongoing command to generosity rather than a false hope that need would vanish.

views.label: Both verses together frame generosity as both an ideal and a lived reality
views.case: Some read these verses as intentionally held together: the vision of a community without poverty motivates obedience, while the realistic acknowledgment of continuing poverty ensures the command to generosity remains urgent and permanent. The release itself is the means by which the ideal of verse 4 is pursued.

views.label: A goal realised in the church
views.case: Luke appears to echo verse 4 when he says of the Jerusalem church, 'There were no needy ones among them,' Acts 4:34. On this reading the promise found a real, if partial, fulfilment when the Spirit created a community that shared its goods.

debates.bearing: The readings fit together. The passage never treats the presence of poverty as an excuse for stinginess; the ongoing reality of need makes structural, generous obedience more urgent, and Acts shows what that obedience can look like.

debates.question: Did the seventh year cancel debts permanently or only suspend their collection?

views.label: Permanent cancellation
views.case: The verb means to let drop or release, and verse 2 says the creditor 'shall cancel what he has loaned.' The fear described in verse 9, that lending just before the seventh year means giving the money away, only makes sense if the debt was truly lost. Nehemiah 10:31 speaks of cancelling every debt, and later Jewish practice treated the release as a real remission.

views.label: A one year moratorium
views.case: Some interpreters argue that since the land lay fallow in the seventh year, Exodus 23:10-11, a farmer could not repay then, so the law suspended collection for that year only. The same verb is used of letting the land rest, which suggests a pause rather than a permanent loss.

debates.bearing: The warning of verse 9 weighs heavily for permanent cancellation, since a mere pause would hardly tempt a lender to refuse a loan. Either way, the law put the needs of a struggling brother ahead of the creditor's rights.

debates.question: How do the servant laws of Exodus 21, Leviticus 25 and Deuteronomy 15 fit together?

views.label: Development and deepening
views.case: Deuteronomy restates Exodus 21 for life in the land, adding the gifts of verse 14, the equal treatment of women, and a motive clause from the exodus. Leviticus 25 treats a different case, the destitute landowner who works as a hired man until the Jubilee restores his land.

views.label: Different kinds of service
views.case: Others distinguish debt service, released after six years, from a fuller sale of the person or land, released at the Jubilee. On this view the laws are complementary provisions for different degrees of poverty, not competing versions of one law.

debates.bearing: All three laws share one conviction: an Israelite belongs first to the LORD who redeemed him, so no other master may own him permanently against his will, Leviticus 25:42. The details differ, but the direction is always toward release.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 7 warns, "you are not to harden your heart," and the BSB footnote gives the literal sense: "make strong" or "make courageous." The verb is amats, the word of Moses' charge, "Be strong and courageous," Deuteronomy 31:6, and of the LORD's charge to Joshua, Joshua 1:6. The quality that should make Israel brave before its enemies can be turned inward to make a heart firm against a poor brother. The paired phrase, "shut your hand," pictures a clenched fist.

The chapter is full of Hebrew's emphatic doubled verb, the infinitive set beside the finite form. Verse 8 says literally "opening you shall open your hand" and "lending you shall lend him"; verse 10, "giving you shall give"; verse 11 again, "opening you shall open." The same construction opened the chapter's promise in verse 5, "if only you obey," literally "if listening you listen." The grammar makes generosity emphatic, not optional.

The "wicked thought" of verse 9 is literally "a word of beliyya'al," a worthless or base word. It is the same term used for the "wicked men" who lead a city to idolatry in 13:13. Moses places the lender's calculation, the year of release is near, in the same moral category as enticement to other gods. The result is that "you look upon your poor brother begrudgingly," literally "your eye is evil toward your brother." The idiom of the evil eye, meaning stinginess, returns in Proverbs 28:22, where "a stingy man" is literally one with an evil eye, while "a generous man" in Proverbs 22:9 is one with a good eye. Jesus uses the same idiom in Matthew 20:15, "are you envious because I am generous?", literally "is your eye evil because I am good?"

Verse 13 forbids sending a freed servant away reqam, "empty-handed." The word deliberately recalls the exodus: God promised that when Israel left Egypt "you will not go away empty-handed," Exodus 3:21, and the Israelites left carrying the Egyptians' silver and gold, Exodus 12:35-36. Deuteronomy 16:16 uses the same word for worshippers who must not appear before the LORD empty-handed. Verse 14 then commands, "furnish him liberally," using the verb anaq, from the word for a necklace, as in Psalm 73:6, "pride is their necklace." The master is to load the departing servant's neck with gifts, sending him away adorned.

The servant who stays is pierced with an awl, martsea, the tool named in Exodus 21:6, and becomes "your servant for life," literally a servant "forever," 'eved olam. And verse 18 values his service at mishneh, "twice," the wages of a hired hand, the same word Isaiah 61:7 uses for the "double portion" God promises His people. Finally, verse 23 commands the blood to be poured out "like water," repeating Deuteronomy 12:24, because "the life of the flesh is in the blood," Leviticus 17:11.

typology.type: The LORD's time of release, verses 1 and 2
typology.fulfillment: Every seventh year the creditor had to let the debt drop, not because the debtor had earned it but because 'the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed.' Isaiah 61:1-2 takes up release as a picture of salvation, and Jesus reads it in Nazareth and says, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing,' Luke 4:21. In Christ God cancels 'the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us,' nailing it to the cross, Colossians 2:14. The escalation is total: the sabbatical release cancelled a neighbour's loan, but Christ releases from the debt of sin owed to God. The type falls short because it had to be repeated every seven years; His release is once for all.

typology.type: The freed servant sent away laden with gifts, verses 12 to 15
typology.fulfillment: The law would not let a released servant leave with nothing, and it grounded that generosity in the exodus, where God brought Israel out with silver and gold. The pattern reaches its fullness in Christ, who not only frees but enriches. 'If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed,' John 8:36, and those set free are given 'every spiritual blessing,' Ephesians 1:3, and the gift of the Spirit. Paul says believers were set free for freedom, Galatians 5:1. The type falls short because the servant went out to an uncertain future; in Christ the freed become sons and heirs, Galatians 4:7.

typology.type: The servant who chooses to stay for love, verses 16 and 17
typology.fulfillment: A servant who loved his master's household could bind himself to it for life, marked by the pierced ear at the door. Isaiah's Servant speaks of an ear opened by the Lord GOD and says, 'I have not been rebellious,' Isaiah 50:5, and Jesus, though Son, 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7. Christ is the Servant who freely binds Himself to His Father's will out of love. Some older interpreters also linked Psalm 40:6, 'my ears You have opened,' to the pierced ear, though the verbs differ and the link is uncertain. The type falls short because the servant's choice served one household, while Christ's service redeems many.

typology.type: The firstborn set apart to the LORD, verses 19 to 23
typology.fulfillment: The firstborn belonged to God because He spared Israel's firstborn when He struck Egypt, Exodus 13:14-15 and Numbers 3:13. Jesus as the firstborn son was presented to the Lord in the temple according to this law, Luke 2:22-23. Paul calls Him 'the firstborn over all creation' and 'firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:15 and 18, and the unblemished animal of verse 21 anticipates 'a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19. The escalation is that He is not only consecrated but offers Himself, and His people become 'the congregation of the firstborn,' Hebrews 12:23. The type falls short because an animal could not choose to be given; Christ offered Himself, Hebrews 9:14.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first by the language of release. The Hebrew idea of letting a debt drop runs from this chapter through the Jubilee of Leviticus 25 to Isaiah 61, where an anointed figure proclaims "liberty to the captives" and "the year of the LORD's favor," Isaiah 61:1-2. When Jesus opens His ministry in Nazareth He reads that very passage and says, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing," Luke 4:21. He presents Himself as the One through whom God's great release arrives.

Jesus fills out that release in His teaching on debt. He teaches His disciples to pray, "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors," Matthew 6:12, using the language of this chapter for sin. In the parable of Matthew 18 a king "had compassion on him, forgave his debt, and released him," Matthew 18:27, and the forgiven servant's refusal to forgive a fellow servant is exactly the hardened heart and shut hand of verse 7. Paul describes the cross as God "having canceled the debt ascribed to us," Colossians 2:14.

The chapter leads to Christ, too, through its motive clause. Israel was to release servants and give generously because "you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you," verse 15. The New Testament grounds Christian generosity in a greater redemption: "though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich," 2 Corinthians 8:9. The freed servant was sent away laden with gifts; those freed by Christ are given the Spirit and made heirs. "If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed," John 8:36.

The servant who chooses lifelong service for love gives a further pattern. Christ, who was Lord, "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant," Philippians 2:7, and the Servant of Isaiah says, "The Lord GOD has opened My ears, and I have not been rebellious," Isaiah 50:5. This is a pattern rather than a prediction, and the link should be held with care, but it fits the New Testament's picture of the Son who serves the Father out of love.

Finally, the firstborn law brings us to the infant Jesus. Luke 2:22-23 records that His parents brought Him to the temple "as it is written in the Law of the Lord: 'Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord.'" The One presented there is also "the firstborn from among the dead," Colossians 1:18, and He offered Himself "unblemished to God," Hebrews 9:14, as the flawless firstborn verse 21 required.

Jesus also quoted verse 11 when a woman poured costly ointment on Him: "The poor you will always have with you, and you can help them whenever you want. But you will not always have Me," Mark 14:7. He did not cancel the duty to the poor; He assumed it. But He placed Himself at the centre, as the One whose death would accomplish the release that every seventh year only pictured.
study.god:
The chapter reveals God as the owner of all things. The release of debts is called "the LORD's time of release," verse 2, and the firstborn belong to Him, verse 19. Israel's land, its people and its herds are held from Him. That is why He can set limits on lending and servitude: no Israelite creditor or master owns anything absolutely. As Leviticus 25:42 puts it, the Israelites are "My servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt."

He is the Redeemer who shapes His people in His own image. Israel is told to release servants and give generously because He redeemed them, verse 15. The pattern of divine action becomes the pattern of human action: as God brought Israel out of slavery laden with gifts, Exodus 12:35-36, so Israel must send out its servants laden with flock, grain and wine, verse 14. Grace received becomes the template for grace given.

He hears the poor. Verse 9 warns that the poor man "will cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin." The same words appear in Deuteronomy 24:15 about unpaid wages. The God who heard Israel's cry in Egypt is still listening, and He hears the cry of the poor even against His own people. There is no neutral ground for the stingy creditor; the needy have an Advocate.

He cares about the heart as well as the hand. God does not merely command the loan; He forbids a grudging spirit, verse 10, and names the lender's calculation as wicked, verse 9. He wants generosity that reflects His own, for He is the God who "loves a cheerful giver," 2 Corinthians 9:7.

He is faithful to bless. The chapter repeats the promise of blessing five times, and it frames generosity not as loss but as trust. Proverbs 19:17 says, "Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender." The God of Deuteronomy 15 invites His people to lend on His credit.

The chapter also holds a tension in God's dealings. He promises that there need be no poor, verse 4, yet He tells Israel plainly that there will always be poor, verse 11. He is both the God of the ideal and the God of the real, holding out a vision of a just community while meeting His people in a world where sin and misfortune persist.

For worship, the chapter joins God's ownership to joy. The firstborn were not given away grimly but eaten "before the LORD" by the whole household, verse 20. Recognising God's claim on everything leads not to anxiety but to feasting, and to open hands.

crossReferences.note: The first form of the servant law: six years of service, release in the seventh, and the pierced ear for a servant who chooses to stay. Deuteronomy 15 restates it for life in the land, adding the generous send off, the exodus motive, and the explicit inclusion of women.

Leviticus forbids treating a destitute Israelite as a slave, because the Israelites are God's servants whom He brought out of Egypt. It shares Deuteronomy 15's conviction that redemption from Egypt limits the power of any human master over a fellow Israelite.

The Sabbath command in Deuteronomy is grounded in 'Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt.' Deuteronomy 15:15 gives the same motive for the seventh year release, showing that the sabbatical year is the Sabbath day applied to debt and servitude.

The LORD quotes this law to the men of Zedekiah's Jerusalem, who freed their Hebrew slaves and then took them back. Because they would not proclaim freedom for their brothers, God proclaims 'freedom' for them to fall by sword, plague and famine. Breaking the release helped bring the exile.

After the exile, Nehemiah confronts nobles who were exploiting their poorer brothers through loans, and he calls them to stop and restore fields and houses. The crisis shows the kind of debt spiral Deuteronomy 15 was designed to break, and later the people pledge to keep the seventh year release, Nehemiah 10:31.

The anointed messenger proclaims liberty to the captives and 'the year of the LORD's favor.' The prophet gathers up the language of sabbatical and Jubilee release into a picture of God's coming salvation, which Jesus claims as fulfilled in Luke 4:18-21.

In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and says it is fulfilled today in their hearing. The release pictured in Deuteronomy 15 every seventh year is announced as arriving in His person and ministry, with good news to the poor at its centre.

A king forgives a servant an unpayable debt, but the servant refuses to release a fellow servant from a small one. The parable reproduces the hard heart and shut hand of Deuteronomy 15:7-9 and shows that those released by God must release others.

Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 15:11, 'The poor you will always have with you,' and adds, 'you can help them whenever you want.' He does not excuse neglect of the poor; He assumes the ongoing duty of the law while pointing to His own coming death.

Luke reports that in the Jerusalem church 'there were no needy ones among them,' because believers sold property and shared the proceeds. The phrase echoes Deuteronomy 15:4, showing the Spirit bringing about in the church the community of open hands the law envisioned.

Mary and Joseph present Jesus in the temple because 'Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord.' The firstborn law of Deuteronomy 15:19 and Exodus 13:2 is applied to Jesus Himself, the firstborn who belongs wholly to God.

John asks how God's love can abide in someone who sees a brother in need and withholds compassion. It is the New Testament form of Deuteronomy 15:7, where Israel is warned not to harden the heart or shut the hand against a poor brother.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God gave humanity a world of abundance and rest. The seventh day was blessed, Genesis 2:3, and the garden supplied what was needed. After the fall came toil, scarcity and the power of the strong over the weak, and by Exodus a whole nation was enslaved. Deuteronomy 15 answers that story by writing the rest of the seventh day into the economy of a redeemed people. Every seventh year debts drop and servants go free.

The chapter looks back to the exodus as its model. God brought Israel out of slavery, not empty but laden with silver and gold. Now Israel is to do for its own poor what God did for them. The land was meant to become a place where the effects of the fall on work and wealth were held in check, where no family would be crushed forever by debt.

The history that follows shows how hard that was. Jeremiah 34 records the release proclaimed and then revoked, and the exile came as the land received the Sabbaths it had been denied, 2 Chronicles 36:21. Nehemiah found the same injustice after the return. The law could describe the release, but it could not produce hearts that would keep it.

Isaiah looked ahead to a greater year of favour, and Jesus announced it as fulfilled in Himself, Luke 4:21. Through His death He cancelled the debt that stood against His people, Colossians 2:14, and through the Spirit He began to form a community in which "there were no needy ones among them," Acts 4:34. The church now lives as a people of released debtors, forgiving as they have been forgiven and opening their hands to the poor, while it waits for the full release still to come.

The new creation completes the chapter. Paul says the creation itself "will be set free from its bondage to decay," Romans 8:21, the release of the seventh year enlarged to the whole cosmos. The firstborn from the dead will have many brothers, Romans 8:29. There will be no poor in that land at last, and no debt, for God will dwell with His people and there will be no more mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:3-4. The promise of Deuteronomy 15:4 will be true without condition.

quiz.q: What must every creditor do at the end of every seven years (vv.1-2)?

options.text: Cancel what he has loaned to his neighbor or brother, since the LORD's time of release has been proclaimed.
options.note: Verses 1-2 state this exact requirement.

options.text: Double the interest owed on the loan.
options.note: The command is cancellation, the opposite of increasing the debt.

options.text: Transfer the debt to the king's treasury.
options.note: No such transfer is mentioned; the debt is simply canceled.

options.text: Nothing is required of creditors.
options.note: Verses 1-2 give an explicit, specific requirement.

quiz.q: What warning does Moses give against withholding help from the poor as the seventh year approaches (v.9)?

options.text: Do not harbor the wicked thought of withholding a loan because the year of release is near, or the poor person's cry to the LORD will bring guilt on you.
options.note: Verse 9 gives this exact warning.

options.text: Lending near the seventh year is entirely forbidden.
options.note: The opposite is commanded; Israel is warned against refusing to lend, not instructed to stop lending.

options.text: The poor person should be reported to the elders instead of helped.
options.note: No such instruction appears; the command is direct, personal generosity.

options.text: No warning is given about this.
options.note: Verse 9 gives an explicit and pointed warning.

quiz.q: What must a master do when releasing a Hebrew servant after six years of service (vv.13-14)?

options.text: Not send him away empty-handed, but furnish him liberally from the flock, threshing floor, and winepress.
options.note: Verses 13-14 state this exact requirement.

options.text: Charge him a release fee before he can leave.
options.note: No such fee is mentioned; the master is instead required to give generously to the departing servant.

options.text: Keep all his previous wages as payment for room and board.
options.note: The text requires generous provision at release, not withholding of wages.

options.text: No instruction is given about how to release him.
options.note: Verses 13-14 give explicit instruction.

quiz.q: What could a servant do if he did not want to leave his master after six years (vv.16-17)?

options.text: Declare his love for his master and household, after which his ear would be pierced with an awl, making him a servant for life.
options.note: Verses 16-17 describe exactly this option and process.

options.text: He had no option but to leave regardless of his wishes.
options.note: Verses 16-17 explicitly describe a voluntary option to remain permanently.

options.text: He could only stay by paying a large fee.
options.note: No fee is mentioned; the process described is the ear-piercing ceremony, not a payment.

options.text: No such option is described.
options.note: Verses 16-17 describe this option in specific detail.

quiz.q: What is Israel commanded to do with the firstborn males of their herds and flocks (vv.19-20)?

options.text: Set them apart to the LORD, not working the firstborn ox or shearing the firstborn sheep, and eat them yearly before the LORD.
options.note: Verses 19-20 give this exact instruction.

options.text: Sell them immediately for maximum profit.
options.note: The instruction is dedication to the LORD, not commercial sale.

options.text: Destroy them completely as unclean.
options.note: The firstborn animals are eaten in a sacred meal before the LORD, not destroyed as unclean.

options.text: No instruction regarding firstborn animals is given.
options.note: Verses 19-20 give explicit, detailed instruction.

questions: God commanded a total, structural reset of debt every seven years, refusing to let poverty become permanent and inescapable. Where do you need to consider forgiving, releasing, or restructuring something owed to you, rather than holding it indefinitely?
Moses warns against the 'wicked thought' of withholding generosity simply because it is inconvenient timing. Where have you delayed genuine generosity while waiting for a more convenient moment?

A released servant was to be sent away 'liberally,' not empty-handed, ensuring a genuine fresh start, not merely technical freedom. Where might you be offering someone freedom in name but not truly equipping them for it in practice?

The firstborn of the flock belonged to the LORD as a reminder that everything ultimately belongs to Him. What first portion, first fruits, or best of what you have are you currently withholding from God?

Moses says 'there will never cease to be poor in the land' (v.11), grounding ongoing generosity in an honest view of the world rather than a naive hope that need will disappear. How does accepting that need will always exist shape a more sustained, rather than occasional, practice of generosity in your own life?

translationNotes.note: 'Remission' translates shemittah, literally 'a dropping' or 'letting fall,' the technical term for this structural cancellation of debt.
This verse's realism about ongoing poverty is echoed by Jesus in Mark 14:7, 'you always have the poor with you,' used there to sharpen rather than excuse the call to generosity.
The ear-piercing ceremony for a servant who chose to remain permanently symbolized a willing, ongoing attachment to the household, a vivid and binding public act rather than a mere legal formality.
